content: Phenoxymethylpenicillin, also known as penicillin V, is a type of penicillin antibiotic that can be administered orally. It is less effective than benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) when targeting Gram-negative bacteria. However, penicillin V is more stable in acidic environments compared to benzylpenicillin, which makes it suitable for oral administration. This antibiotic exhibits bactericidal activity against microorganisms that are sensitive to penicillin, specifically during their active multiplication phase. Its mechanism of action involves the inhibition of cell-wall peptidoglycan biosynthesis. Penicillin V is ineffective against bacteria that produce beta-lactamase enzymes, such as many strains of Staphylococci. Its antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria is comparable to that of benzylpenicillin, but it is significantly less effective against Gram-negative bacteria. Penicillin V works by killing penicillin-sensitive bacteria during their active growth phase. It achieves this by inhibiting the synthesis of cell-wall mucopeptides. However, it does not act against penicillinase-producing bacteria, which include numerous strains of staphylococci. In laboratory studies, penicillin V has demonstrated high activity against certain bacteria, including staphylococci (excluding penicillinase-producing strains), streptococci (groups A, C, G, H, L, and M), and pneumococci. Other bacteria that are sensitive to penicillin V in vitro include Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Bacillus anthracis, Clostridia, Actinomyces bovis, Streptobacillus moniliformis, Listeria monocytogenes, Leptospira, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Additionally, Treponema pallidum is highly sensitive to penicillin V.
